extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in psychology and humor studies; scholars of cognition and comedy practitioners seeking theory-level explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Benign Violation Theory of humor: when and why circumstances elicit amusement and laughter, specifying necessary appraisals, factors that make violations benign, timing considerations, and illustrative domains (puns, sarcasm, slapstick, tickling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a psychological state characterized by the positive emotion of amusement and the tendency to laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the target phenomenon the theory seeks to explain: positive emotion (amusement) plus the behavioral tendency to laugh. The account aims to predict when this state will arise across varied circumstances (from puns to play).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when (1) a circumstance is appraised as a violation, (2) the circumstance is appraised as benign, and (3) both appraisals occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three appraisals are necessary; removing either appraisal causes the humor attempt to fail. This triadic condition is the core evaluative rubric for whether an instance will produce amusement/laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation (appraisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation refers to anything that threatens one’s beliefs about how things should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include threats to physical well-being (e.g., feigned aggression), identity (insults), social norms (flatulence), cultural norms (awkward greetings), linguistic norms (puns, malapropisms), logic norms (absurdities), and moral norms (disrespectful behavior). The theory notes an evolutionary origin in threats to physical safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness (appraisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a violation to produce humor it also needs to seem OK, safe, acceptable, or benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors that make a situation seem benign include: a playful motivational state; cues that the situation should not be taken seriously; the presence of an alternative norm or an explanation that resolves the violation; a safe environment; psychological distance (physical, temporal, social, hypothetical); and a low commitment to the person or norm threatened. These factors are the evaluative criteria for perceived benignness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity, timing, and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the appraisal that there is a violation and the appraisal that everything is benign need to occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simultaneity explains why timing, brevity, and surprise are important in comedy. If appraisals are not simultaneous, humor fails (no perceived violation → boredom; no perceived benignness → confusion or offense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic wordplay criterion (puns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns and other wordplay break one linguistic norm, convention, or rule (violation), while simultaneously adhering to another norm, convention, or rule (benign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why people with strong knowledge of language (bookish people) enjoy puns: they detect the violated rule and also recognize the alternative norm that renders the instance acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcasm involves saying one thing but meaning the opposite, violating conversational norms while relying on cues to signal benign intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sarcasm requires perceivers to detect the speaker’s true intention via cues like exaggerated tone. It fails (is not funny) when listeners do not detect the intended meaning or disapprove of the speaker’s intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup–punchline/joke-structure criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Setup or punch-line jokes operate when the setup that seems illogical or incorrect (violation) is resolved or explained (benign) by the punch line, or when an innocent observation (benign) is succeeded by a disparaging answer (violation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes that lack a violation sound like normal sentences; jokes that are not benign don’t make sense or seem stupid or offensive. This provides an evaluative test for joke construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical play / tickling criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling and rough-and-tumble play are physical attacks (violation) that often don’t hurt or cause harm (benign) for the person who experiences humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-tickling does not elicit laughter because there is no perceived threat (no violation). If the victim distrusts the aggressor, the situation is not benign and laughter may not occur. Trust and perceived harmlessness are key evaluative elements here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Slapstick creates painful-seeming circumstances (violation) that are not actually painful (benign), at least for the person who experiences humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor arises when the victim is not actually hurt or the audience does not care about the victim’s well-being. If the audience cares about the person who is hurt, the situation ceases to be benign and will probably not elicit laughter. Conversely, mundane non-violations (e.g., casually walking past a banana peel) are unlikely to provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences in humor perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Both what seems wrong (violation) and what seems OK (benign) depend on people’s physiological vulnerabilities, desired identity traits, values, cultural background, language, and understanding of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains variation in humorous responses (e.g., a baby farting might be normal to the baby, hilarious to an older sibling, and embarrassing to a mother). Use this criterion to predict or evaluate variability across audiences.
